# KV Cache: A Technical Overview

## What Is KV Cache?

In transformer-based language models, inference proceeds autoregressively—each new token is generated one at a time, conditioned on all previously generated tokens. During this process, the model computes key and value vectors for every token position through self-attention layers. These computations are expensive, involving matrix multiplications across the model's hidden dimension.

KV cache is an optimization that stores these computed key and value tensors from previous forward passes, avoiding redundant recomputation when generating subsequent tokens. Instead of recalculating keys and values for the entire context history each time a new token is produced, the model retrieves pre-computed values from cache and only computes the KV pairs for the newly appended token.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

Without KV caching, generating a sequence of N tokens requires O(N²) operations in the attention mechanism, since each step reprocesses all prior tokens. With KV caching, this reduces to O(N), because each position's keys and values are computed exactly once and reused.

This efficiency gain becomes critical as context windows expand. Modern models support context lengths ranging from tens of thousands to over a million tokens. Without caching, the computational cost would grow quadratically, making long-context generation prohibitively slow or impossible within practical resource constraints. KV caching transforms what would be an intractable problem into something manageable, enabling applications like extended document analysis, multi-turn conversations, and code repositories as context.

However, KV cache introduces memory tradeoffs. Storing KV tensors for long contexts consumes significant GPU memory, proportional to context length, head count, and hidden dimension size. This has motivated research into KV cache compression techniques, including quantization, selective retention strategies, and specialized hardware
